market_context: United States; celiac disease and gluten-free labeling
title: Which Foods Have Gluten, and Which Are Naturally Gluten-Free?

seo.title: Foods With Gluten and Naturally Gluten-Free Foods
seo.meta_description: Wheat, barley, and rye contain gluten. Rice, corn, potatoes, quinoa, beans, produce, plain meat, fish, eggs, and dairy are naturally gluten-free.
seo.search_intent: Identify gluten-containing foods and foods that are naturally free of gluten.

excerpt: Gluten is found in wheat, barley, rye, and their related varieties or derivatives. Rice, corn, potatoes, quinoa, beans, fruits, vegetables, plain meat, fish, eggs, and dairy are naturally gluten-free, but processed foods can add gluten ingredients or cross-contact.
content_html:
A gluten-free diet does not require avoiding every grain, every starch, or every carbohydrate. Gluten is the protein mixture associated with wheat, rye, barley, and their crossbred relatives; rice, corn, potatoes, quinoa, buckwheat, legumes, fruits, vegetables, plain animal foods, and many other staples are naturally gluten-free. The complication comes after processing, because a naturally gluten-free ingredient can be combined with a gluten-containing ingredient or exposed to cross-contact.

Wheat, barley, and rye are the core grains to recognize

Wheat appears under many familiar names: durum, semolina, spelt, farro, einkorn, emmer, bulgur, couscous, and conventional wheat flour all belong to the wheat family. Rye and barley also contain gluten proteins relevant to celiac disease. Foods made from these grains include ordinary bread, pasta, many crackers, baked goods, some breakfast cereals, seitan, malt products, and conventional beer. Triticale, a wheat-rye cross, also belongs on the avoid list for a strict gluten-free diet.

Many staple foods are gluten-free before processing

Rice, corn, potatoes, sweet potatoes, quinoa, buckwheat, millet, sorghum, amaranth, beans, lentils, peas, fruits, and vegetables do not naturally contain gluten. Plain meat, poultry, fish, eggs, milk, yogurt, cheese, oils, nuts, and seeds are also naturally free of gluten when no gluten-containing ingredients have been added. This is why a nutritious gluten-free diet can be built from ordinary foods rather than relying on specialty replacement breads and cookies.

Oats are naturally different but cross-contact is common

Oats are not wheat, barley, or rye, and pure oats do not contain the same gluten proteins. The practical problem is that oats can be contaminated with wheat, barley, or rye during growing, transport, milling, or packaging. In the United States, oats can be labeled gluten-free if the finished food meets FDA's gluten-free rule, including less than 20 parts per million of unavoidable gluten. Some people with celiac disease also appear to have individual sensitivity to oat avenin, so medical guidance may matter when oats are being introduced after diagnosis.

Prepared foods require more label reading than whole foods

Soy sauce made with wheat, gravies thickened with flour, malt flavoring, breaded foods, soups, seasoning blends, imitation meats, desserts, and some processed meats can introduce gluten where the basic food might otherwise be gluten-free. Cross-contact matters in kitchens too: a shared fryer full of breaded crumbs, a toaster used for wheat bread, pasta water, cutting boards, and flour dust can all be relevant for celiac disease. “No wheat” is not the same as “gluten-free,” because barley or rye may still be present.

A U.S. gluten-free label has a regulatory meaning

FDA permits a voluntary gluten-free claim only when the food meets the rule's ingredient restrictions and any unavoidable gluten is below 20 ppm. A naturally gluten-free food such as plain rice does not need to carry the claim to be gluten-free, while a processed grain product may benefit from the assurance because cross-contact risk is higher. Start with the ingredient's natural source, then use the ingredient list, gluten-free claim, and cross-contact information to decide whether the finished food fits a strict gluten-free diet.

Celiac disease also makes preparation conditions important. A naturally gluten-free potato can become unsuitable if it is coated with wheat flour or fried in oil shared with breaded foods. Oats deserve special attention because they are often contaminated with wheat, barley, or rye during growing and processing; people with celiac disease generally need oats specifically labeled gluten-free. Wheat allergy is a separate diagnosis, so a “gluten-free” label answers a different question than “wheat-free.”

Malt is another common source of confusion. Barley malt, malt extract, and malt flavoring made from barley are not gluten-free unless a product meets the gluten-free rule through an allowed formulation and testing. Soy sauce, seasoning blends, gravies, and imitation meats can also contain wheat. The safest shortcut for a packaged product is not to memorize every possible recipe but to read the ingredient and allergen information and rely on a gluten-free claim when strict avoidance is required.

faq.question: Does rice have gluten?
faq.answer: No. Plain rice is naturally gluten-free, although prepared rice products can contain added gluten ingredients or encounter cross-contact.

faq.question: Are oats gluten-free?
faq.answer: Pure oats are not wheat, barley, or rye, but cross-contact is common. For celiac disease, products labeled gluten-free provide clearer assurance that the finished food meets the U.S. rule.

faq.question: What does gluten-free mean on a U.S. label?
faq.answer: FDA requires the food to meet ingredient restrictions and any unavoidable gluten to be below 20 parts per million.
